blocks.text: Most marine animals are hypotonic to their environment. This means that external environment has a much higher solute (salt) concentration than their internal tissues. Water constantly leaves their bodies via osmosis through the gills and skin. Salts continuously diffuse from the environment into their bodies. In addition, they have excess of salts in the body due to drinking of sea water.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Most marine animals are invertebrates, and these are osmoconformers, isotonic with sea water (see 13.2.1). It is the marine bony fishes, and other marine vertebrates that are osmoregulators, that are hypotonic to sea water; the rest of this section (gills, drinking sea water, chloride cells) describes them.

To compensate for the water loss, marine animals drink seawater continuously. They also conserve water by producing very small amounts of highly concentrated urine. To remove the excess salts, specialized chloride cells in the gills use energy (ATP) to actively pump salts out of the blood and back into the environment. They also remove excess salts through their kidneys. Some marine fishes also have special salt excreting glands in rectum called rectal glands. These glands remove salts from blood into the digestive tract which are then eliminated along with faeces.

blocks.alt: Two fish side by side, (a) on the left and (b) on the right, with the key centred below; blue arrows show water, red arrows salts. (a) Freshwater fish: water and salts enter the mouth with food, salts are actively transported in at the gills, water enters through gills and other parts, and dilute urine leaves. (b) Marine fish: food and drinking water enter the mouth, salts are excreted through the gills, water is lost through gills and other parts, and concentrated urine leaves.
blocks.caption: Figure 13.4: Osmoregulation in (a)- freshwater and (b)- marine water (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 13.4).
blocks.long_description: Labels in (a): Food; Active transport of salts (red arrow into the gills); Entry of water through gills and other parts (four blue arrows into the body); Dilute urine (a long blue and a short red arrow at the vent). Labels in (b): Food & drinking water; Excretion of salts through gills (red arrow out of the gills); Water loss through gills and other parts (three blue arrows out of the body); Concentrated urine (a short blue and a long red arrow). The key shows a blue arrow for movement of water and a red arrow for movement of salts.
